topics.topic: Development of practical skills in physics

questions.prompt:
A student plots a graph to test a proposed linear relationship between two physical quantities.
(a) Explain how the gradient can be used to determine a physical constant. (2)
(b) Describe two ways to reduce uncertainty in the gradient. (2)
(c) Explain why a straight-line graph alone does not prove the proposed model is exact. (2)
hints: A large gradient triangle reduces percentage reading uncertainty.
questions.solution:
(a) Rearrange the model into $y=mx+c$ and identify the constant from the theoretical expression for $m$. [M1 A1]
(b) Use a wide range of values and a best-fit line/large triangle; repeat measurements where appropriate. [B1 B1]
(c) Experimental uncertainty and a limited data range may hide small systematic deviations from the model. [B1 B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to investigate the relationship between a marble's speed v and the distance x it rolls on carpet, given ½mv² = Fx, and how to find F. (4)
questions.solution:
Release marble down a ramp; measure speed with a light gate at the bottom [B1]
Measure distance travelled on carpet with a metre rule [B1]
Vary release height; repeat and average [B1]
Plot v² against x; F = ½m × gradient [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe an experiment to determine the force constant of an elastic cord, including the graph plotted. (4)
questions.solution:
Hang cord from a clamp with a ruler alongside [B1]
Add masses in steps and measure extension each time [B1]
Plot force against extension [B1]
Force constant = gradient of the linear region [B1]

questions.prompt:
A graph of T² against L for a pivoted rod has gradient 2.70 s² m⁻¹ = 8π²/3g.
(i) Calculate g. (2)
(ii) A worst-fit line has gradient 2.84 s² m⁻¹. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in g. (2)
(iii) Comment on accuracy compared with 9.81 m s⁻². (1)
questions.solution:
(i) g = 8π² ÷ (3 × 2.70) [M1]
= 9.75 m s⁻² [A1]
(ii) (2.84 − 2.70) ÷ 2.70 × 100 [M1]
= 5.2% [A1]
(iii) 0.6% from true value – within uncertainty, so accurate [B1]

questions.prompt: Show that a graph of ln N against d for gamma absorption, N = N₀e^(−μd), is a straight line, and state what the gradient and intercept give. (3)
questions.solution:
ln N = ln N₀ − μd [M1]
Gradient = −μ [A1]
Intercept = ln N₀ [B1]

questions.prompt: A count is N = 300 ± 40. Calculate ln N and its absolute uncertainty. (2)
Define accuracy and precision. (2)
questions.solution:
Accuracy: how close a value is to the true value [B1]
Precision: how close repeated measurements are to each other [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to determine the period of an oscillating rod accurately. (2)
questions.solution:
Time 20 oscillations and divide; repeat and average [B1]
Use a fiducial marker at the equilibrium position [B1]

questions.prompt: A cube's side is measured with a 2% uncertainty. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in its volume and density (mass uncertainty negligible). (2)

(i) A ball falls 1.20 m in 0.50 s from rest. Calculate g. (1)
(ii) A ball rolls 1.900 m from rest down a 30° ramp in 0.90 s. Calculate g, ignoring rotation. (2)
(iii) A stopwatch has a reaction-time uncertainty of about 0.1 s. Explain which value is less reliable. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) g = 2 × 1.20 ÷ 0.50² = 9.6 m s⁻² [B1]
(ii) a = 2 × 1.900 ÷ 0.90² = 4.7 m s⁻² [M1]
g = 4.7 ÷ sin 30° = 9.4 m s⁻² [A1]
(iii) Free fall: 20% uncertainty in t, giving 40% in g – much less reliable than the ramp (11% in t) [B1]

questions.prompt: Wire diameter readings are 0.460, 0.450, 0.455, 0.495 and 0.455 mm. Explain how d = 0.455 ± 0.005 mm is obtained. (3)
questions.solution:
0.495 mm is anomalous and is excluded [B1]
Mean of the remaining four = 0.455 mm [B1]
Uncertainty = half the range = (0.460 − 0.450) ÷ 2 = 0.005 mm [B1]

questions.prompt:
Light intensity in jelly follows I = I₀e^(−μx).
(i) Show that ln I against x gives a straight line with negative gradient. (2)
(ii) Intensity falls from 80 units to 20 units over 4.0 mm. Calculate μ. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) ln I = ln I₀ − μx [M1]
Compare with y = mx + c: gradient = −μ, intercept ln I₀ [A1]
(ii) μ = ln(80/20) ÷ 4.0 [M1]
= 0.35 mm⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt:
N capacitors (each C) in parallel discharge through N resistors (each R) in series.
(i) Show that the halving time is T = (ln 2)N²RC. (2)
(ii) A graph of T against N² has gradient 0.69 s. With C = 1000 μF, calculate R. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Total capacitance NC, total resistance NR, so time constant N²RC [M1]
Halving time = ln 2 × time constant [A1]
(ii) R = 0.69 ÷ (0.693 × 1000 × 10⁻⁶) [M1]
= 1.0 × 10³ Ω [A1]

questions.prompt: In the experiment above, the sixth "1000 μF" capacitor is actually two 470 μF capacitors in parallel. State the type of error and its effect on the N = 6 result. (2)
questions.solution:
Systematic error [B1]
Total capacitance is too small, so T for N = 6 is too short [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) For LEDs, eV₀ = hc/λ. Gradient of V₀ against 1/λ is 1.24 × 10⁻⁶ V m. Calculate h. (3)
(ii) Calculate the percentage difference from 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. (1)

A 600 lines mm⁻¹ grating gives a second-order maximum a distance y from the centre on a screen x away.
(i) Explain why the gradient of y against √(x² + y²) equals sin θ. (1)
(ii) The gradient is 0.78. Calculate the wavelength. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse = y ÷ √(x² + y²) [B1]
(ii) d = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m [M1]
λ = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.78 ÷ 2 [M1]
= 6.5 × 10⁻⁷ m [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) State the derived SI unit of the area between loading and unloading curves on a force-extension graph. (1)
(ii) Explain the significance of this area for a rubber cord. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Joule [B1]
(ii) Energy dissipated (as heat) per loading cycle [B1]
Rubber warms up; useful for absorbing vibrations/shocks [B1]

questions.prompt: Strip thickness readings are 1.86, 1.88, 1.85, 1.89 and 1.88 mm. Calculate the percentage uncertainty. (2)
For a vibrating wire, √W = 2f√μ L. The gradient is 2.81 N^½ m⁻¹ and μ = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg m⁻¹. Calculate f and comment on 50.0 Hz. (3)
Explain how the force from one atom could be used to estimate total gas pressure. (2)
questions.solution:
Multiply by the number of atoms moving in that direction (N/3) [B1]
Divide total force by wall area [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a pressure-temperature graph for a gas at constant volume gives absolute zero. (2)
questions.solution:
Straight line extrapolated to p = 0 [B1]
Temperature intercept is absolute zero (≈ −273 °C) [B1]

questions.prompt:
A length is measured as (2.40 ± 0.05) m.
(a) Calculate the percentage uncertainty. (2)
(b) The length is squared to obtain an area proportional to $L^2$. Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the area. (2)
(c) Explain the difference between a random and a systematic error. (3)
hints: For powers, multiply fractional uncertainty by the power.
questions.solution:
(a) Percentage uncertainty $=0.05/2.40\times100=2.08\%$. [M1 A1]
(b) For $L^2$, percentage uncertainty $\approx2\times2.08=4.17\%$. [M1 A1]
(c) Random errors vary unpredictably between readings and can be reduced by repeats; systematic errors shift readings consistently and are not removed by averaging. [B1 B1 B1]
questions.subtopic: Development of practical skills in physics

questions.prompt: Express the pascal in SI base units. (2)
questions.solution:
Pa = N m⁻² [M1]
= kg m⁻¹ s⁻² [A1]

questions.prompt: Show that eV = hc/λ is homogeneous by finding the base units of h. (2)
questions.solution:
h = eVλ/c: J × m ÷ m s⁻¹ = J s [M1]
= kg m² s⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt: Show that a = −ω²x is homogeneous. (2)
questions.solution:
Left: m s⁻² [B1]
Right: s⁻² × m = m s⁻² [B1]

questions.prompt: Given the ohm is kg m² s⁻³ A⁻², find the base units of resistivity. (2)
questions.solution:
Ω m [M1]
kg m³ s⁻³ A⁻² [A1]

questions.prompt: Classify these as scalar or vector: weight, mass, velocity, kinetic energy. (2)
questions.solution:
Vectors: weight, velocity [B1]
Scalars: mass, kinetic energy [B1]

questions.prompt: A resultant force of 5.0 N acts at an angle; the vertical component balances a 3.0 N weight. Calculate the horizontal component. (2)
Write 25 pF in farads in standard form. (1)
Times of 2.31, 2.35, 2.28 and 2.34 s are recorded. Give the mean and absolute uncertainty. (2)
Derive the SI base units of resistance. (2)
questions.solution:
Volt = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹ [M1]
Ohm = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻² [A1]

questions.prompt: Show that P = ½ρAv³ is homogeneous. (2)
questions.solution:
RHS: kg m⁻³ × m² × m³ s⁻³ [M1]
= kg m² s⁻³, the same as watts [A1]

questions.prompt: Show that T² = 2π²m/k is homogeneous. (2)
questions.solution:
k = kg s⁻² [M1]
m/k = kg ÷ kg s⁻² = s² [A1]

questions.prompt: Give the SI base units of the Boltzmann constant. (2)
questions.solution:
J K⁻¹ [M1]
kg m² s⁻² K⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt: Convert 1 kWh into joules and give its base units. (2)
Convert a Hubble constant of 68 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ into s⁻¹ (1 Mpc = 3.09 × 10²² m). (2)
An experiment gives h = 6.3 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Calculate the percentage difference from 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. (1)
Classify displacement, kinetic energy, weight and temperature as scalars or vectors. (2)
questions.solution:
Vectors: displacement, weight [B1]
Scalars: kinetic energy, temperature [B1]

questions.prompt: Show that s = ½gt² is homogeneous. (2)
questions.solution:
RHS: m s⁻² × s² [M1]
= m, matching the LHS [A1]

questions.prompt: Give the unit of gravitational field strength in terms of N. (1)
Explain why the watt isn't a unit of energy. (1)
questions.solution: It's a unit of power (J s⁻¹) [B1]

questions.prompt:
A body of mass 2.0 kg is pulled horizontally by a force of 12 N. A resistive force of 3 N acts in the opposite direction.
(a) Calculate the acceleration. (3)
(b) Starting from rest, calculate the speed after 4.0 s assuming constant acceleration. (2)
(c) Explain one limitation of the constant-resistance model. (2)
questions.solution:
(a) Resultant force $=12-3=9$ N. $a=F/m=4.50$ m s$^{-2}$. [M1 M1 A1]
(b) $v=u+at=0+4.50\times4=18.00$ m s$^{-1}$. [M1 A1]
(c) Real drag generally changes with speed/environment, so it is unlikely to remain constant. [B1 B1]

questions.prompt:
A 15 g ball is dropped. From the v-t graph, the tangent at 0.25 s gives an acceleration of 6.0 m s⁻².
(i) Calculate the resultant force. (1)
(ii) Calculate the drag at that instant. (3)
Explain why a ball filled with sand reaches a higher terminal velocity than the same hollow ball. (2)
questions.solution:
Heavier ball has greater weight [B1]
Must reach a higher speed for drag to equal weight [B1]

questions.prompt: A car at 20 m s⁻¹ has a reaction time of 0.60 s and a stopping distance of 40 m. Calculate the braking deceleration. (3)
questions.solution:
Thinking distance = 12 m [M1]
Braking distance = 28 m [M1]
a = 20² ÷ (2 × 28) = 7.1 m s⁻² [A1]

questions.prompt:
A 30 g ball with 1.0 J of kinetic energy is launched horizontally from 1.5 m above the ground.
(i) Show that its speed is about 8 m s⁻¹. (1)
(ii) Calculate its horizontal range. (3)
A 20 000 kg train at 40 m s⁻¹ sees an obstruction 150 m ahead. Reaction time is 0.50 s; braking force 150 kN. Show that it stops in time. (4)
State what the gradient and the area under a velocity-time graph represent. (2)
A car drips oil at regular time intervals. Describe the pattern of drips for constant speed and for acceleration. (2)
questions.solution:
Equal spacing for constant speed [B1]
Increasing spacing when accelerating [B1]

questions.prompt:
Road markings are 40 m apart and the speed limit is 110 km h⁻¹.
(i) Convert 110 km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹. (2)
(ii) Calculate the time to travel between markings. (1)

A 57.0 g ball leaves a racket at 30.0 m s⁻¹ at 70° above the horizontal.
(i) Show that its maximum height is about 40 m. (3)
(ii) Calculate its kinetic energy at maximum height. (2)

A sandbag is released from 17 m above the ground moving horizontally at 8.0 m s⁻¹.
(i) Calculate its time to fall. (2)
(ii) Calculate its horizontal displacement. (2)

A rocket's engine stops 50 s after launch, when it moves at 3.1 km s⁻¹ at 75° to the horizontal.
(i) Estimate the extra height it gains after the engine stops, assuming constant g. (2)
(ii) Estimate the height gained while the engine fires, assuming uniform acceleration. (1)
(iii) Calculate g at about 530 km altitude (R_E = 6400 km) and comment on the assumption. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) uᵧ = 3.0 × 10³ m s⁻¹ [M1]
h = (3.0 × 10³)² ÷ (2 × 9.81) = 4.6 × 10⁵ m [A1]
(ii) Average vertical speed 1.5 km s⁻¹ × 50 s = 7.5 × 10⁴ m [B1]
(iii) g = 9.81 × (6400/6930)² = 8.4 m s⁻² [M1]
g falls by about 15%, so H is underestimated [A1]

questions.prompt:
A 120 g load falls from rest through 0.80 m, then stops in 25 ms.
(i) Calculate its speed just before impact. (2)
(ii) Calculate the average resultant force during stopping. (2)
A falling ball passes two light gates 0.52 m apart at 1.20 m s⁻¹ and 3.40 m s⁻¹. Calculate g. (2)
Explain the effect of an upward slope on a car's braking distance. (2)
questions.solution:
Component of weight acts down the slope, opposing motion [B1]
Greater deceleration, so shorter braking distance [B1]

questions.prompt: Braking distance ∝ initial KE. A car braking from 10 m s⁻¹ takes 18 m. Find the distance from 25 m s⁻¹. (1)
Calculate the distance an object falls from rest between t = 0.20 s and t = 0.30 s. (1)

A wooden cylinder (5.0 × 10⁻³ kg, diameter 1.0 cm, length 7.0 cm) falls 0.30 m from rest.
(i) Calculate the wood's density. (2)
(ii) Calculate its speed on reaching the water. (2)

An arrow is launched at 68 m s⁻¹ at 11° towards a target 90 m away at the same height.
(i) Show the time to maximum height is about 1.3 s. (1)
(ii) Calculate how far above the target's centre it passes. (2)

An object leaves an aircraft moving horizontally at 220 m s⁻¹ and falls 2500 m.
(i) Show it takes about 23 s. (1)
(ii) Calculate its final velocity and angle to the vertical. (3)

A 2.1 × 10⁵ kg train has a 190 kN driving force below 6.0 m s⁻¹.
(i) Show its acceleration is about 1 m s⁻². (1)
(ii) Calculate the distance to reach 6.0 m s⁻¹. (2)
A spring (k = 60 N m⁻¹) launches an 80 g car up to 0.20 m high. Calculate the minimum compression. (2)

(i) Equal and opposite forces of 400 N act on a screwdriver blade 6.0 mm wide. Calculate the torque. (1)
(ii) State the principle of moments. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) 400 × 6.0 × 10⁻³ = 2.4 N m [B1]
(ii) For a body in equilibrium, sum of clockwise moments [B1]
= sum of anticlockwise moments about any point [B1]

questions.prompt:
Wind at 10 m s⁻¹ hits a 5.0 m × 2.0 m tent side at right angles (air density 1.2 kg m⁻³).
(i) Calculate the mass of air hitting it in 3.0 s. (2)
(ii) The air is deflected through 90°, losing all its velocity towards the tent. Calculate the force. (2)
A 10 kg suitcase moves at constant speed up a belt inclined at 25°. Calculate the friction and normal contact forces. (3)
A probe of volume 1.7 m³ sits on Venus where the atmosphere has density 65 kg m⁻³ and g = 8.87 N kg⁻¹. Calculate the upthrust. (3)

A water rocket's internal pressure is 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa and atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. The nozzle area is 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². Calculate the upward force and the initial acceleration of the 0.55 kg rocket. (3)
State the two conditions for an object to be in equilibrium. (2)
questions.solution:
Resultant force is zero [B1]
Resultant moment is zero [B1]

questions.prompt: An object falls through water. Describe how its acceleration changes as it approaches terminal velocity. (2)
questions.solution:
Drag increases with speed, so acceleration decreases [B1]
Acceleration becomes zero at terminal velocity [B1]

questions.prompt: A car of weight 9300 N freewheels down a 5° slope at a maximum speed of 30 m s⁻¹. Drag is F = kv². Show that k is about 1. (3)

(i) The car above (k = 0.90 kg m⁻¹) has engine power 75 kW. Calculate its maximum speed on level ground. (2)
(ii) Explain why doubling the power doesn't double the maximum speed. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) v³ = 75 000 ÷ 0.90 [M1]
v = 44 m s⁻¹ [A1]
(ii) P = kv³, so v ∝ P^(1/3) [B1]
Doubling P increases v by only a factor of 1.26 [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to find the centre of mass of a flat irregular sheet. (3)
questions.solution:
Hang the sheet freely from a pin through a hole near the edge [B1]
Use a plumb line to draw a vertical line [B1]
Repeat from another point; centre of mass is where lines cross [B1]

questions.prompt: A block of density 800 kg m⁻³ floats in water. Calculate the fraction above the surface. (2)
A uniform 4.0 m beam of weight 200 N rests on supports at its ends. A 600 N load sits 1.0 m from the left. Calculate each support force. (2)
Forces of 15 N act on opposite sides of a 4.0 cm diameter shaft. Calculate the torque. (1)

(i) Describe and explain the motion of a sphere released in a fluid until terminal velocity. (3)
(ii) Calculate the terminal velocity of a 1.0 mm diameter steel sphere (7800 kg m⁻³) in oil (920 kg m⁻³, η = 0.050 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹) using v = 2gr²(ρs − ρf)/9η. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Initially accelerates at g as drag is zero [B1]
Drag increases with speed, so resultant force and acceleration fall [B1]
Weight = drag + upthrust, giving constant terminal velocity [B1]
(ii) v = 2 × 9.81 × (5.0 × 10⁻⁴)² × 6880 ÷ (9 × 0.050) [M1]
= 0.075 m s⁻¹ [A1]

questions.prompt: Glue with breaking stress 130 kPa holds a 7.8 N weight. Find the minimum area. (1)

A 1100 kg car is towed at constant speed up a 10° slope against 300 N friction, rising 120 m.
(i) Show the weight component down the slope is about 1900 N. (1)
(ii) Calculate the tow force. (1)
(iii) Calculate the work done by it. (2)
Liquid pressure at the bottom of a floating cylinder is 1.9 × 10³ Pa at depth 15 cm. Calculate the liquid's density. (2)
A 1200 kg cylindrical drum with base area 0.79 m² floats upright in water. Calculate its depth below the surface. (2)

(i) A 9.0 nC ball sits between plates 8.0 cm apart at 4.0 kV. Show the electric force is 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ N. (1)
(ii) Its weight is 0.030 N on a 120 cm thread. Show its sideways displacement is about 1.8 cm. (2)

A 20 000 kg train reaches 40 m s⁻¹ with a 300 kW engine.
(i) Show that the minimum time to reach this speed is about 1 minute. (2)
(ii) Calculate the driving force at 40 m s⁻¹ at full power. (1)
A cord of force constant 500 N m⁻¹ is stretched 6.3 cm. Show that it stores about 1 J. (2)
A pendulum bob is released from 0.20 m above its lowest point. Calculate its maximum speed. (2)
A torch capacitor stores 3.2 J. Estimate how long it can light a 40 mW LED and state one assumption. (3)
questions.solution:
t = 3.2 ÷ 0.040 [M1]
= 80 s [A1]
Assumes all stored energy is transferred to the LED / constant power [B1]

questions.prompt: A motor uses 500 J to lift a 2.0 kg mass 15 m. Calculate its efficiency. (2)
Describe the energy changes as a mass on a spring moves from its lowest point, through equilibrium, to its highest point. (3)
questions.solution:
At the lowest point elastic PE is maximum, KE zero [B1]
At equilibrium KE is maximum [B1]
At the top GPE is maximum and KE zero; some energy lost to air resistance [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) A 120 kN bridge section is raised so its centre of mass rises 6.3 m in 90 s. Calculate the average power. (2)
(ii) Suggest why the motor's maximum power is several times larger. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) P = 120 × 10³ × 6.3 ÷ 90 [M1]
= 8.4 kW [A1]
(ii) Friction/inefficiency losses and extra power needed to accelerate it [B1]

questions.prompt:
Wind at 8.0 m s⁻¹ carries 1.2 MJ s⁻¹ of kinetic energy through a turbine (ρ = 1.3 kg m⁻³).
(i) Calculate the mass of air incident per second. (2)
(ii) Use P = ½ρAv³ to calculate the blade length. (2)
Each turbine receives 1.2 MW and is 42% efficient. Calculate the minimum number for 50 MW of output. (2)
Derive KE = p²/2m. (2)
A motor lifts a load at constant speed. Describe how its kinetic and gravitational potential energy change. (2)
questions.solution:
Kinetic energy constant [B1]
Gravitational potential energy increases linearly with time [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a ball's kinetic energy isn't zero at the top of its flight. (1)
questions.solution: Horizontal velocity is unchanged (no air resistance) [B1]

questions.prompt: A 12 kg seat swings 10 m from the axis at 0.82 rad s⁻¹. Calculate its kinetic energy. (2)

A 400 N force moves 80.0 cm to raise a 1200 kg car by 2.0 cm.
(i) Calculate the work done by the force. (1)
(ii) Find the speed ratio. (1)
(iii) Calculate the efficiency. (2)
A 4.5 N force stretches a spring 3.2 cm. Calculate the elastic energy. (1)
A train's output is 4.0 MW from a 25 kV supply. Calculate the current. (1)
Compare energy stored per kg in sand raised 1 km (70% efficient) with wax heated 18 °C → 70 °C, melting at 51 °C (c_solid 2.6, c_liquid 3.0 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L = 160 kJ kg⁻¹, 95% efficient). (3)

A wire of original length 1.2 m and cross-sectional area 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ m$^2$ extends by 0.8 mm under a tensile force of 120 N.
(a) Calculate the stress. (2)
(b) Calculate the strain. (2)
(c) Hence calculate Young modulus. (2)
questions.solution:
(a) Stress $=F/A=8.000\times10^{7}$ Pa. [M1 A1]
(b) Strain $=\Delta L/L=6.667\times10^{-4}$. [M1 A1]
(c) $E=\text{stress}/\text{strain}=1.200\times10^{11}$ Pa. [M1 A1]

questions.prompt:
A cable of diameter 4.0 mm breaks under a force of 2.0 kN.
(i) Define ultimate tensile strength. (1)
(ii) Calculate the breaking stress. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Maximum stress a material can withstand before breaking [B1]
(ii) A = π × (2.0 × 10⁻³)² = 1.26 × 10⁻⁵ m² [M1]
σ = 2000 ÷ 1.26 × 10⁻⁵ [M1]
= 1.6 × 10⁸ Pa [A1]

questions.prompt:
A cable extends 2.0 mm under 1.0 kN within its elastic region.
(i) Calculate its force constant. (2)
(ii) Explain why more work is done extending it from 3.0 to 4.0 mm than from 1.0 to 2.0 mm. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) 1000 ÷ 2.0 × 10⁻³ [M1]
= 5.0 × 10⁵ N m⁻¹ [A1]
(ii) Force is larger over the later extension, so the area under the graph is greater [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to check that a cable has a uniform cross-section. (2)
questions.solution:
Measure diameter with a micrometer [B1]
At several points and orientations along the cable [B1]

questions.prompt: A stress-strain graph is linear up to 200 MPa at a strain of 0.0010. Calculate the Young modulus. (2)
Distinguish elastic and plastic deformation. (2)
questions.solution:
Elastic: returns to original shape when the load is removed [B1]
Plastic: permanently deformed [B1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the stress in a wire of area 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ m² supporting a 5.0 kg mass. (2)

(i) A rubber cord's lower end moves from 1.80 m to 0.81 m above the floor under 6.0 N. Calculate the extension. (1)
(ii) Loading and unloading curves are curved and don't coincide. Discuss whether Hooke's law applies. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) 0.99 m [B1]
(ii) Graph isn't a straight line through the origin [B1]
Extension not proportional to force – Hooke's law doesn't apply [B1]

questions.prompt: A 2.0 m wire of diameter 0.50 mm extends 2.0 mm under 40 N. Calculate its Young modulus. (3)
questions.solution:
A = 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m² [M1]
Stress = 2.04 × 10⁸ Pa; strain = 1.0 × 10⁻³ [M1]
E = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa [A1]

questions.prompt: Define the elastic limit and the ultimate tensile strength. (2)
questions.solution:
Elastic limit: maximum stress beyond which the material doesn't return to its original length [B1]
UTS: maximum stress the material can withstand before breaking [B1]

questions.prompt: Wire B, of the same material as A, has twice the length and twice the diameter. Find the extension ratio B : A for the same load. (2)
A spring of stiffness 40 N m⁻¹ is stretched by a 6.0 N force. Calculate the energy stored. (2)
Describe two factors affecting accuracy when cord extension is measured via a pulley system. (2)
questions.solution:
